chunks: PFET and NFET on together: shoot-through. The question: What happens if you turn both the PFET and NFET on the same side at the same time? How do you prevent this? 1
Shoot-through is when the top and bottom switches in the same leg are on at the same time.
That connects the supply straight to ground through both switches, with no load in the way. The current spikes, the switches heat up, the supply sags and parts often die.
It can happen even when the control logic looks correct, so you add a deliberate gap, called dead time, plus other safeguards.
Picture a canal lock with a gate at each end. If the upstream gate and the downstream gate are open together, water rushes straight through and floods everything.
The safe rule is to close one gate fully before you open the other. Dead time is the pause between "close" and "open".
The analogy leaves out one trick: a fast voltage jump at the middle node can push a gate open by itself, like a gust slamming a door.
With both gates asserted the current runs from V M through Q P and Q N to ground and never touches the load.
The only limits are the FETs' saturation currents, the loop inductance and the supply impedance.
Leg: a high-side and a low-side switch sharing one output node. Dead time: a short interval, tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, when both switches are off.
Turn-off delay: the time a switch takes to actually stop conducting after its gate is told to turn off.
Miller turn-on: a fast voltage jump at the output leaks through the FET's internal capacitance into its gate and briefly turns the "off" switch on.
CMOS inverter: a PFET and NFET with joined gates, which has the same overlap issue on a small scale.
A 24 volts leg has two switches, each with 20 milliohms of on-resistance. If both are fully on, the ideal current is 24 over (0. 02 plus 0. 02) equals 600 amps.
Real FETs limit their own current, so it is lower, but still tens of amps or more.
Add 100 nanoseconds of dead time at each transition and neither switch is on while the other turns off, so the short never forms. That is the whole idea.
"Turning on the PFET and NFET in the same leg shorts the supply to ground through two on-resistances, so you get big current spikes, heat, rail droop and often a dead FET.
It happens with overlapping gate edges, tied gates, mismatched turn-off and turn-on delays, or Miller-coupled dv/dt.
I prevent it with separate gate drives and dead time, a driver with built-in shoot-through protection, faster turn-off than turn-on, stiff gate pull-downs, and current limiting as a backstop."
